title: My tennis coach's 5 words
author: Kate Sotsenko
summary: Sotsenko builds a redefinition of productivity around five words from her childhood tennis coach: just put the ball in. The piece opens with a workshop for leaders in which more than eighty percent agreed that productivity means doing more and doing it faster, a definition she held herself until burnout put her on three weeks of enforced rest. Lying on the sofa she noticed the contradiction in her own history, that a punishing junior tennis schedule never broke her while a fast, deadline-hitting corporate career did. Her explanation is that tennis is organised around results and endings while desk work is organised around volume, and volume is infinite. She traces the doing-more definition back to factory work, where output per unit of time was a fair measure, and argues it stopped fitting once people were hired for judgement and relationships rather than throughput. The practical prescription is a single question asked before every email, deck and day: what is the end goal, because it is impossible not to overwork when you do not know when the game ends.
points: Sotsenko argues that defining productivity as doing more makes work structurally unfinishable, which is why it colonises the whole day.
She contrasts a gruelling junior tennis schedule that never caused burnout with a fast corporate career that did, locating the difference in goals rather than hours.
The doing-more definition is traced to factory production, where fixed processes made output per unit of time a legitimate measure.
Her operational fix is to open every task by defining what done looks like, which bounds the effort before it starts.
She frames intentional decision making as a trainable skill rather than a personality trait, naming it Good Busy.
quotes: When I was 13, my tennis coach noticed that every time I received an easy ball — opponent in a difficult position, point literally won — I'd hit it as hard as I could. Most times, I'd miss.
But now I know that the idea of productivity as doing more is why work never ends. Why it follows you from the moment you open your eyes in the morning until your head hits the pillow at night.

In tennis, nobody thinks about doing more. Everyone thinks about the goal. Nobody cares how many balls you hit in an hour. All that counts is the result — the training session goal, the next match goal, the season goal.
More is infinite. No matter how much you squeeze, how many boxes you ticked, how many emails you replied to, it never feels enough. It's never done.

My work-life balance changed when I stopped aiming to do more and focused on just putting the ball in . In no way is it easy. It's a skill — the skill of making intentional decisions, keeping focus on the right ball and the goal.

It's like playing a tennis match without knowing the end game. You'll keep playing until the cows come home. You'll keep going for as long as you can until you're exhausted and wondering when it ends.
The end gives your busyness direction and a clear destination. When you know how the game ends, you find smarter ways to win it — you're more resourceful than you think — and stop playing.
